q: What is the main aim of protectionist trade policies?
options: Remove barriers to foreign competition
Shield domestic producers from foreign competition
Give foreign producers exclusive access to the market
Prevent domestic firms from selling at home
feedback: Protectionist policies limit foreign competition to benefit domestic producers. Whether those policies benefit the country overall requires considering their costs as well as their benefits.
commonError: Confuses protectionism with opening a market to foreign competition.

q: What is the economy's potential output?
options: Output when every worker works as many hours as possible
Output that eliminates all unemployment
Output that can be sustained at normal resource use
Output that consumers would buy if all prices were zero
feedback: Potential output is the level of production the economy can sustain with normal use of labor and other resources. It does not require zero unemployment or round-the-clock production.
commonError: Confuses sustainable potential output with the greatest physically possible output.

q: During long-run macroeconomic self-adjustment, what happens to wages and prices that were slow to change in the short run?
options: They gradually adjust to economic conditions
They remain permanently fixed by their earlier contracts
They all fall to zero as markets adjust
They can change only if the government sets them
feedback: Wages and prices can be slow to respond in the short run. As contracts are renewed and expectations change, they adjust and help move production back toward potential output.
commonError: Treats short-run wage and price stickiness as permanent.

q: During a recession caused by a fall in aggregate demand, high unemployment tends to put what pressure on nominal wages over time?
options: Upward pressure from a shortage of workers
No pressure because wages can never change
Upward pressure from stronger demand for labor
Downward pressure from weak demand for labor
feedback: When demand for labor is weak and many workers are seeking jobs, nominal wages face downward pressure. This may appear as slower wage growth rather than immediate wage cuts.
commonError: Reverses the wage pressure associated with high unemployment.

q: When output is temporarily above potential, strong demand for workers tends to put what pressure on nominal wages over time?
options: Downward pressure because labor is less scarce
Upward pressure as employers compete for workers
No pressure because wages are permanently fixed
Downward pressure as fewer employers seek workers
feedback: Strong demand for labor makes workers harder to recruit and retain, putting upward pressure on nominal wages. Rising labor costs are part of the economy's adjustment back toward potential output.
commonError: Reverses the wage pressure associated with output above potential.

q: How does easy entry of new sellers support competition in a market?
options: It guarantees that existing sellers earn a profit
It allows existing sellers to set a common price
It gives buyers more alternatives to existing sellers
It prevents buyers from switching between sellers
feedback: New sellers give buyers additional alternatives. The possibility of entry also limits existing sellers' ability to charge high prices without attracting competition.
commonError: Treats easy entry as protection for existing sellers rather than a source of competition.

q: How can a commercial bank create deposit money when it makes a loan?
options: By crediting the borrower's checking account
By printing new currency in its own name
By collecting a tax from the borrower
By recording the loan as government spending
feedback: The bank records a loan and credits a spendable deposit to the borrower. It does not need to print currency to create that deposit.
commonError: Confuses bank-created deposits with newly printed currency.

q: In the simple money-multiplier model, why does keeping loan proceeds as cash limit further deposit expansion?
options: Cash automatically becomes additional bank reserves
The original borrower no longer owes the loan
Banks must pay a higher interest rate on all deposits
Less money is redeposited to support further lending
feedback: The simple deposit-expansion process relies on loan payments returning to banks as deposits. Money kept as cash outside the banking system interrupts that process.
commonError: Assumes money kept outside banks supports the same redeposit process as money returned to banks.

q: In monopolistic competition, what does product variety mean?
options: Every firm produces an identical good
Consumers can choose among differentiated products
Every firm must charge the same price
Consumers can buy from only one seller
feedback: Product variety means that consumers can choose products with different features, quality, style, or locations. Those differences can help consumers find products that better match their preferences.
commonError: Confuses differentiated products with identical products.

q: Which feature would make monopolistic competition a poor model of a market?
options: Many firms offer competing brands
Consumers value differences between products
Only one firm sells the product
New firms can enter the market relatively easily
feedback: Monopolistic competition assumes many sellers offering differentiated products. A market served by a single seller fits monopoly rather than monopolistic competition.
commonError: Overlooks the many-seller assumption of monopolistic competition.

q: What does statutory tax incidence describe?
options: Who is legally responsible for sending the tax payment to the government
Who ultimately loses purchasing power because of the tax
How much the tax changes the quantity traded in the market
How the government chooses to spend the tax revenue
feedback: Statutory incidence identifies the party legally responsible for paying the tax to the government. That party does not necessarily bear the entire economic burden.
commonError: Confuses legal responsibility for paying a tax with its economic burden.

q: What does economic tax incidence describe?
options: Which government agency receives the tax payment
Which party the law requires to submit the tax payment
Which public programs receive the tax revenue
How the tax burden is divided between buyers and sellers
feedback: Economic incidence concerns who bears the tax burden through the prices buyers pay and sellers receive. It can differ from the legal assignment of the tax.
commonError: Treats the legal assignment of a tax as a complete description of who bears its cost.

q: A tax causes the total price paid by buyers, including the tax, to rise. What does this indicate?
options: Sellers necessarily bear the entire tax burden
Buyers bear some of the tax's economic burden
The tax has no economic burden on either side
The government bears the tax instead of buyers or sellers
feedback: Buyers bear part of a tax's burden when it raises the total price they pay. This can happen even when sellers are legally responsible for sending the tax payment to the government.
commonError: Ignores a higher buyer price when identifying the economic burden of a tax.
